Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.

p.seg: In the past, Róng Chéng Shì,
... [ ] Zūn Lú Shì, Hè Xū Shì, [ ]
Gāo Xīn Shì, Cāng Jié Shì,
Xuān Yuán Shì, Shén Nóng Shì,
Hún Dùn Shì, and Fú Xī Shì possessed the world.
They did not pass it to their sons
but instead passed it to the worthy.
Their virtue was clear and pure,
those above loved those below,
they unified their will,
and laid down their weapons.
... and they assigned offices according to talent.
Thereupon, the mute and deaf held torches,
the blind played the zither,
the lame guarded the gates,
the dwarves made arrows,
the hunchbacked used divination to choose residences,
the stooped handled counting,
those with goiters boiled salt at home,
the bald fished in the marshes,
... the disabled and abandoned were not [ ].
All people of lowly status
were taught and instructed,
given drink and food,
and the hundred officials were made to serve them.
And every month they were invited.
Therefore, at that time,
... there were no annexations [ ].
... When the [ ] Shì possessed the world,
they were generous in love
and light in taxation.
They applied their own physical strength to work for the common people.
... [ ] Thereupon, they did not reward or punish,
did not execute or kill.
The states had no hungry people,
and on the roads there were none who died prematurely.
Those above and below, the noble and the lowly,
each obtained their proper rank.
Those from beyond the four seas came as guests,
those within the four seas were upright.
The birds and beasts came to court,
the fish and turtles offered tribute.
What was possessed and what was lacked were exchanged.
They corrected the governance of the world for nineteen years
and ruled as kings over the world for thirty-seven years,
until their final passing.
In the past, Yáo lived between Dān Fǔ and Jué Líng.
Yáo walked with generosity and offered sacrifices at the proper times.
Without being exhorted, the people exerted their strength;
without executions or killings, there were no thieves or robbers.
He was very lenient, yet the people were submissive.
Thereupon, within an area of a hundred lǐ,
he led the people of the world,
and they came to support and establish him
as the Tiān Zǐ.
Thereupon, within a radius of a thousand lǐ,
[thereupon] they held their tablets and took their proper positions.
From the four directions, they submitted in harmony,
and he cherished them so as to bring in the people of the world.
His governance was orderly without rewards,
he assigned offices without bestowing titles.
There was no coercion of the people,
and he governed disorder without weariness.
Therefore it is said:
... worthiness reached [ ].
This is how worthiness was viewed:
Treading upon the earth and bearing heaven on the head,
being sincere in righteousness and trustworthiness,
meeting between heaven and earth,
and encompassing everything within the four seas.
He could complete all tasks,
and thus was established as the Tiān Zǐ.
Yáo gave this instruction:
"Let them present themselves,
and I shall peer through the opening
to seek the worthy
and abdicate to them."
Yáo offered the world to a worthy person,
but the worthy of the world
were none of them able to accept it.
The lords of the ten thousand states
all offered their states to the worthy.
... [ ] the worthy,
but none of the worthy were able to accept it.
Thereupon, the people of the world
considered Yáo to be good at promoting the worthy,
and ultimately established him.
In the past, Shùn plowed at Lì Qiū,
made pottery by the banks of the Hé,
fished at Léi Zé,
showed filial piety in nourishing his father and mother,
and by being good to his kin,
it reached the people of the state.
Yáo heard of this
and praised his conduct.
Thereupon, Yáo prepared fifteen chariots
to go three times to follow Shùn in the fields.
Thereupon, Shùn for the first time was relieved of holding the hoe and spade,
and was dressed in grand attire to be seated.
Master Yáo faced south,
and Shùn faced north.
Shùn then began to speak to Yáo
about the Way of Heaven, Earth, and the people.
When speaking of governance,
it was pleasingly simple yet implemented;
when speaking of music,
it was pleasingly harmonious and enduring;
when speaking of rites,
it was pleasingly broad and not contrary.
Yáo was then pleased.
Yáo [became old,
his vision was not clear],
and his hearing was not sharp.
Yáo had nine sons,
but he did not make his sons his successors.
Seeing the worthiness of Shùn,
he desired to make him his successor.
[Shùn then declined five times in favor of the worthy of the world,
and having no other choice,
only then did he dare to accept it.]
Shùn governed for three years;
the mountains and hills were not cleared,
and the floodwaters did not flow properly.
He then established Yǔ as the Sī Gōng.
After Yǔ had received the command,
he wore clothes made of grass and a hat made of bamboo leaves,
... [ ] his face was dry and rough,
and no hair grew on his shins.
He opened blockages and made the waters flow.
Yǔ personally held the basket and shovel
to embank the marsh of Míng Dū,
and cleared the obstructions of the Nine Rivers.
Thereupon, Jiá Zhōu and Xú Zhōu first became habitable.
Yǔ opened the Huái and Yí,
so they flowed eastward into the sea.
Thereupon, Qīng Zhōu and Jǔ Zhōu first became habitable.
Yǔ then opened the Lóu and Tāng,
so they flowed eastward into the sea.
Thereupon, Yōu Zhōu first became habitable.
Yǔ then opened the Three Rivers and Five Lakes
so they flowed eastward into the sea; thereupon, Jīng Zhōu and Yáng Zhōu first became habitable.
Yǔ then opened the Yī and Luò, and combined the Chán and Jiàn,
so they flowed eastward into the Hé.
Thereupon, Yù Zhōu first became habitable.
Yǔ then opened the Jīng and Wèi,
so they flowed northward into the Hé.
Thereupon, Yōng Zhōu first became habitable.
Yǔ then followed south of the Hàn to name five hundred valleys,
and followed north of the Hàn to name five hundred valleys.
Once the dwellings of the people of the world were settled,
and they could plow and eat,
he established Hòu Jì as the Jùn.
After Hòu Jì had received the command,
he ate in the wild
and slept in the wild.
He cultivated the grains and raised livestock on the soil.
In five years, there was an abundant harvest.
The people had surplus food,
and there was nothing they sought that they did not obtain.
The people then offered sacrifices.
When arrogance and extravagance began to arise,
he established Gāo Yáo as the Lǐ.
After Gāo Yáo had received the command,
he distinguished the qi of Yin and Yang
and heard their litigations.
In three years, there were no more people in the world who had litigations.
The world was in great harmony and equality.
Shùn then desired to gather the qi of Heaven and Earth
and listen to its use.
He then established Zhì as the Yuè Zhèng.
After Zhì received the command, he created the six pitch-pipes and six companion pipes,
distinguished the five tones,
and determined the sounds of men and women.
At that time,
pestilence did not arrive,
ominous omens did not occur,
disasters and calamities departed and vanished.
The birds and beasts were fat and large,
and the grasses and trees grew vigorously.
In the past, Heaven and Earth assisted Shùn
and protected the good.
This was the state of things.
Shùn then became old,
his vision was not clear,
and his hearing was not sharp.
Shùn had seven sons,
but he did not make his sons his successors.
Seeing the worthiness of Yǔ,
he desired to make him his successor.
Yǔ then declined five times in favor of the worthy of the world,
and having no other choice,
only then did he dare to accept it.
When Yǔ administered the government for three years,
he did not produce leather armor,
he did not sharpen metal weapons,
he did not distribute arrows,
the fields had no weeds,
the houses were not empty,
. there were no taxes at the passes or markets.
Yǔ then followed the mountains, hills, plains, and marshes where towns could be established
and made them populous and prosperous;
thus he used what was near to understand what was far,
removed harshness and practiced simplicity,
followed the desires of the people,
and gathered the benefits of Heaven and Earth.
For this reason, those who were near delighted in his rule,
. and those who were far came of their own accord.
Those within the Four Seas were reached,
. and those beyond the Four Seas all requested to offer tribute.
Only then did Yǔ first create titles and banners
to distinguish their left and right,
. and to ensure the people were not confused.
The banner of the East featured the sun,
the banner of the West featured the moon,
the banner of the South featured a snake,
the banner of the center featured a bear,
. and the banner of the North featured a bird.
Only then did Yǔ first practice frugality:
clothes were not fresh and beautiful,
food did not have double flavors,
the court did not use carriages for greeting,
the mortar did not over-polish the rice,
. and the cook did not break the bones.
He established the filial seasons ( ? ),
and for the regions made the Three Proclamations,
saving the discipline of sounds:
three proclamations for the East,
three proclamations for the West,
three proclamations for the South,
three proclamations for the North,
to protect the streams and valleys,
and cross the wide rivers.
High mountains were climbed,
and thick forests were entered,
. and there he administered the government.
Thereupon he first established ranks and distributed salaries,
to yield to those who came after.
Orderly and harmonious,
it was said that virtue quickly urges ? ? ?
.... [ ] outer skin ?
Yǔ then set up a drum in the court,
. so that the people who had lawsuits or petitions could strike it.
Upon the striking of the drum,
Yǔ would certainly come out quickly;
in winter he did not dare to decline because of the cold,
. and in summer he did not dare to decline because of the heat.
He spoke personally [personal example]
.... [ ] deep place
said:
As for the Sage,
his life is a gift of nourishment,
and his death is a gift of burial.
He removes harshness and evil,
. and thus he makes his name.
Yǔ had five sons
but did not make his sons his successors.
Seeing the worthiness of Gāoyáo,
. he wished to make him his successor.
Gāoyáo then yielded five times to the worthy of the world
and finally claimed illness.
. He did not come out and died.
Thereupon Yǔ yielded to Yì,
. but Qǐ then attacked Yì and took the position for himself.
[Qǐ] ruled the world for sixteen {years}
. and then Jié arose.
Jié did not follow the Way of his former kings,
.... made his own [made his own changes] [ ]
... [ ] At that time,
the strong and weak did not listen to pleas,
the many and few did not listen to lawsuits,
. and the affairs of Heaven, Earth, and the four seasons were not cultivated.
Tāng then extensively created tax records,
. to tax the passes and markets.
The people then had reason to be resentful,
and cruel diseases began to arise,
+. whereupon the mute, deaf, lame, blind, those with goiters, (and other ailments), and the hunched first appeared.
Tāng then planned precautions and sought the worthy,
. and he appointed Yī Yǐn to be his assistant.
After Yī Yǐn had received his orders,
. he took up arms to forbid violence.
He pretended to win over the people
and then went astray;
not measuring that his strength was insufficient,
he raised an army to attack the Mínshān Shì,
taking their two daughters, Yǎn and Wǎn.
+ (The women?) left their state for the North,
. [ ] built the Qīnggōng,
constructed the Xuánshì,
decorated the Yáotái,
. and established the Yùmén.
. His pride and arrogance were of this state.
Tāng heard of this,
. and thereupon he was cautious, took precautions, and summoned the worthy.
He bestowed virtue and kindness without relying on it,
and accumulated this for thirty years
. until he was capable of action.
Only when things were like this and yet the other would not change,
. did he then proceed to attack him.
Ascending from the Róng (É? ) pass,
entering through the North Gate,
.. standing in the center [ ]
. Jié then fled to the Lìshān Shì.
Tāng again followed and attacked him,
descending from the Míngtiáo pass,
. to attack the gate of Gāoshén.
. Jié then fled to the Náncháo Shì.
Tāng again followed and attacked him,
and Jié then fled,
. leaving for the wilds of Cāngwú.
Tāng thereupon summoned the armies of the Jiǔzhōu
+ to unify n within the Four Seas,
thereupon the soldiers of the world rose in great numbers,
and thus he destroyed the clans,
executed the families,
and ruined the groups of the wicked.
. Thus they submitted.
... [ ] robbers and thieves.
For this reason he gained the masses
. and ruled the world.
Tāng's line ruled the world for thirty-one generations,
. and then Zhòu arose.
Zhòu did not follow the Way of his former kings
and made his own changes.
Thereupon he built the Nine-layered Terrace,
placed a vat of charcoal beneath it,
and placed a round beam over it,
making the people walk upon it.
Those who could succeed did so,
but those who could not succeed
. fell in and died.
. Those who did not follow his orders were then put in shackles.
. Thereupon he made three thousand metal shackles.
Having made the metal shackles,
he also made a lake of wine
. and took great pleasure in wine.
From dusk through the night he practiced debauchery,
. and did not listen to the government of his state.
Thereupon nine states rebelled against him:
. Fēng, Gǎo, Zhōu, Shíyì, Yú, Lù, Lí, Chóng, and the Mìxū Shì.
Wén Wáng heard of it,
and said:
"Though the ruler lacks the Way,
would a minister dare not to serve him?
Though a father lacks the Way,
would a son dare not to serve him?
Who is the Son of Heaven that one could rebel against?"
Zhòu heard of this,
and released Wén Wáng from beneath the Xiàtái
and questioned him,
saying:
"Can the nine states be made to come back?"
Wén Wáng said:
. "They can."
X Wén Wáng then wore plain robes
to go to the nine states.
Seven states came to submit,
. but Fēng and Gǎo did not submit.
Wén Wáng then raised an army and headed toward Fēng and Gǎo.
Three times the drums beat
and they advanced,
and three times the drums beat
and they retreated.
He said:
"Those I know are many and pitiable.
If one man lacks the Way,
what crime have the common people committed?"
The people of Fēng and Gǎo heard this
. and then surrendered to Wén Wáng.
Wén Wáng maintained the ancient times
and taught the people the seasons.
He fully knew the benefits of high and low, fertile and barren lands.
He knew the Way of Heaven
and the benefits of the Earth,
. and he ensured the people were not ill.
In the past, when Wén Wáng assisted Zhòu,
. it was in this manner.
Wén Wáng passed away,
. and Wǔ Wáng ascended the throne.
Wǔ Wáng said:
"As for those of perfect virtue,
. I shall take their place with pleasure.
As for those next to them,
. I shall attack them and take their place.
Now Zhòu practices no Way,
destroys and abandons the common people,
and shackles the feudal lords.
Heaven is about to execute him,
. and I shall assist Heaven's majesty."
Wǔ Wáng then prepared one thousand leather chariots
and ten thousand armored soldiers.
On the day of Wùwǔ,
he crossed at Mèngjīn
and reached the area between Gòng and Téng.
At night, he met with the armies of the Zhūhóu at the wilds of Mù.
